tagline: Slate sidewalks and marble underfoot along Route 30 through the Taconics
intro: Stone Valley’s Route 30 corridor follows the Mettawee drainage through the Taconic Mountains and passes along Lake Bomoseen’s eastern shore in Hubbardton. Vermont Tourism presents the Stone Valley Byway as a journey through the region’s stone heritage, linking the Dorset Playhouse, Poultney’s historical museums and a Revolutionary War battlefield. In the Mettawee Valley, farmland opens out at the Pawlet Flats, where hay and corn grow; surrounding forests produce lumber and maple syrup.

The road’s number has a history broader than this byway. From 1922 to 1926, New England Route 30 ran from Granville, New York, through Poultney and north to Alburg. When northern sections became U.S. highways in 1926, Vermont subsequently extended the Route 30 designation southeast to Brattleboro. A later change left a mark at the former Jenks Tavern in East Rupert: its attached barn was demolished when Route 30 was realigned in 1948.

Driving south from Hubbardton, follow Lake Bomoseen’s eastern shore toward Castleton, cross U.S. 4 and continue to Poultney. The road passes the eastern edge of Lake St. Catherine State Park, then runs through Wells, Pawlet and Dorset toward Manchester Center. In Dorset, locally quarried marble faces some Church Street sidewalks; in Manchester Center, Route 30 reaches the roundabout.
notice: Compare Poultney’s slate sidewalks and fences with Dorset’s locally quarried marble sidewalks.

moments.title: Hubbardton Battlefield
moments.text: On July 7, 1777, British troops caught the American rear guard at Hubbardton during the retreat from Fort Ticonderoga. Most of the American army had continued toward Castleton, while Seth Warner’s rear guard stopped to rest and gather stragglers. German reinforcements helped scatter the Americans, but British losses ended pursuit of the main army. A monument commissioned in 1859 began a later chapter of commemoration. Vermont acquired battlefield land in the 1930s, and interpretive signs along the battlefield trail identify locations in the fighting. The visitor center’s permanent exhibit places the battle within the wider story of the Revolutionary War.

moments.title: Lake Bomoseen
moments.text: Slate quarry holes and rubble piles survive in Bomoseen State Park on the lake’s western shore. Their material began as ocean-floor clay, compressed into shale and transformed by heat and pressure as the Taconic Mountains rose. The quarries supplied the West Castleton Railroad and Slate Company, whose complex stood between Glen Lake and Lake Bomoseen. Several slate buildings and foundations remain in the park. The lake itself was formed by glaciation and lies in both Castleton and Hubbardton. A self-guided Slate History Trail brochure is available at the park’s contact station.

moments.title: Poultney
moments.text: Poultney’s slate history runs underfoot and along its streets. The town was a center of the slate industry, and slate sidewalks and fences remain part of its streetscape. Vermont Tourism singles out the Poultney Historical Society’s museums as part of the Stone Valley Byway. Nearby, Route 30 passes along the eastern edge of Lake St. Catherine State Park.

moments.title: Dorset
moments.text: Dorset’s marble appears in the village’s everyday surfaces: some Church Street sidewalks are faced with stone quarried locally. The Congregational Church also has a marble-faced exterior, in Gothic Revival style. The village began as an agricultural community, then gained from demand for marble for projects across the country. Limited water power and poor rail connections constrained its nineteenth-century growth, and East Dorset overtook it in importance. The historic village center stands at the junction of Route 30, Church Street and Kent Hill Road. Wood-frame commercial buildings and mainly nineteenth-century houses cluster in the historic center alongside those marble surfaces.

sources.label: Vermont Tourism, 72 Hours in Rutland and Vermont’s Stone Valley
